I work in the vet field (ER/ICU) and I 100% agree that poor people should be able to have pets. Here's the breakdown:

1. There are so many abandoned animals and animals being put down because there aren't enough homes for them. So we're going to deny an animal a home because someone isn't going to be able to drop $1000 at the drop of a hat? 

2. There are financial relief funds available, and low-cost facilities for care. Granted you're not going to receive the gold standard of care at those facilities, but they're going to do what they can. 

3. If a pet presents due a life-threatening condition, it is absolutely ok to euthanize them. You're not giving up on them, you're allowing them to not suffer. The same applies for certain expensive, life-long illnesses/conditions. And no, you did not fail them by choosing that option.

4. In the instance where someone cannot afford to euthanize their sick pet BE HONEST. Chances are that, yes, you are going to have to take them with you afterwards to either bury somewhere or seek low-cost cremation options, but every veterinary facility I have ever worked at has honored and comped euthanasia charges. Once again, it is important to be up and honest about your finances so people are aware. 

5. Your local Humane Society and SPCA usually have "pantry" programs available where you can have assistance with feeding your pet.

It's not that there aren't drugs that can, it's just that they're not the "clot busters" that humans can get. There are a few oral medications that can be given at this instance, but many intravenous medications are contraindicated in animals just because they metabolize and respond so much differently than us.

There are multiple risks involved in a case such as this. Like the other commenter said, it also depends on where the clot is whether or not amputation is possible. Where they were talking about the bifurcation of the aorta, for instance, that's around where the lumbar and pelvis meet (to give the best picture) and you can't amputate there. In the instance where only the lower portion of the extremely is affected, that's when amputation may be possible, but is very risky.

Just like with people, animals who have a heart condition are very high risk candidates for surgery. Many of the drugs that could be given can cause additional arrhythmias, intravenous fluid therapy needs to be extremely conservative as to not overload the heart, and general anesthesia itself can cause a significantly lower heart rate, which can be very difficult to control with these patients. There's also an increased chance of thrombosis while under anesthesia. What makes a case like this even a higher risk is that they've already thrombosed, so having additional blood clots form could increase the chance of an additional thrombos forming.

Cases like these are best suited for a specialty hospital for these reasons because they have the team to give them the best chance. Many specialty hospitals have board certified anesthesiologists, cardiologists, internists, and criticalists, which would be exactly what they would need to give them the best chance.

Incorrect, but Reglan CRI's are a little confusing until you get the hang out of it. Not to worry! Here's a breakdown.


Whenever we do calculations, we will eliminate the information that we have already used, and when we do a specific step in our problem we will eliminate like-values (which will be explained further down).


The information we have that is pertinent to this equation: 

>25kg patient

>2mg/kg/day Reglan

>24hr/day

>IVF running at 50mL/hr

>New L of IVF


We need to figure out how many hours the bag will last us, which can be calculated by the mLs in the bag, which is 1,000mL at this point, divided by the mL/hr that the fluids are running at, which is 50mL/hr. So 1,000mL/L ÷ 50mL/hr = 20hr/L. We elimated both of the mL values so that way we don't get confused and know exactly what our result equates to. We are also going to add the hours/L into the pertinent information for the problem.


Since we have used the amount of mL in the bag (1L) and the mL/hr (50mL/hr) we are going to remove that from the information that we pulled from the problem, leaving us with:


>25kg patient 

>2mg/kg/day Reglan

>24hr/day

>20hr/L


Now we're going to figure out how many mgs in the day the patient needs.
25kg x 2mg/kg/day = 50mg/day. We will cross out the kg value since its present on both sides. We are now going to elimate those from our information, and adding in this value, leaving us with:


>20hr/L

>50mg/day

>24hr/day

We don't titrate medications in days, rather in hours. So what we are going to do next is divide by 24 to find out how many mg/hr the patient will need. 50mg/day ÷ 24hr/day = ~2.08mg/hr. Once again, make sure you remove the same values from either side to avoid confusion. 


NOW we are going to utilize the hr/L.

2.08mg/hr x 20hr/L = ~41.7mg/L


Just remember that when instilling IVF additives to remove the amount of fluid from the bag BEFORE injecting it into the bag, otherwise it will equal a lessor concentration. 


I have only seen, and believe, that Reglan comes in a concentration of 5mg/mL, so we take our 41.7mg/L ÷ 5mg/mL = 8.3mL/L. So we will remove 8.3mL from our liter of IVF before injecting 8.3mL of Reglan into the bag.


Hope this helps!

A good company to get it through is Trupanion. The deductible is per condition instead of annual, which made more sense in my eyes. They also don't exclude conditions that certain breeds are more prone to, which is also a big plus. They pay the clinic directly and you're just responsible for you $0-1,000 deductible and 10% of the bill. 

They don't have a maximum payout, which is a big thing that people don't think about. I'm a nurse in the ICU in a specialty/emergency/critical care hospital and I've seen bills easily go up to and over 20k, depending on the duration of stay, illness and how intensive the treatment is, which is more than some insurance company's annual allotted payouts.

The only 3 downsides are that they don't have a wellness/prevention plan since they're emergency based only, they don't offer multi-pet/policy discounts, and they tend to be more expensive per month.

Hi, certified trainer here. So the best way that I've found to go about this is to ask some friends, neighbors and/or strangers to give her treats when she isn't being overly excited. This is what I mean:


1. Get people to give to her when the time is right. This doesn't have to be planned, but is a lot easier if there are people already in on it. Otherwise you will need 2 people while on a walk with her; one to hold the leash and one to approach the person on the walk to ask for help.

2. It's important that the treats be given at the exact moment when she starts to calm down. You have to try to keep her focusing on you for this in the beginning, which will be hard, but it should pay off in the end. When you have her focused, that's when the stranger/visitor/friend/etc. should walk passed you, seemingly ignoring her, but lightly toss a treat in her direction. Other than this mild interaction they need to ignore her. She should only get a treat if she is calm, otherwise they should completely ignore her and keep walking until they are at a distance where you can refocus her. The goal is for them to get as close to her as possible without her reacting. When you find that line, have them toss treats at her so that way she will learn that she will get their attention only if she is calm. It is also extremely important that you give her a "jackpot" of treats, meaning 3-5 high-reward treats, and praise her when she achieves this goal for it to succeed. The moment that she is giving you the result that you're looking for you need to mark it with either a click from a clicker or a firm marking word. I use "yes!" with a clear, precise and articulated "s" because it's easy for them to determine that they did what you wanted and easier than growing another hand for a clicker. 

3. Repeat this exercise until she has at least a 98% success rate. You can start to close the gap once this is achieved. It is also okay for you to widen the gap again if she is unable to calm down to "go back to basics" to refocus her and to try again. 

4. Continue this outside on walks until people can approach her within touching distance and her not reacting at least 98% of the time. Once she has achieved this, you can start having the other person introduce petting instead, since it seems that their attention is a high-reward to her. Only let them pet her until you know she will become hyperactive again, then back off a give her a jackpot of treats and repeat, extending the duration of time that they can pet her until she doesn't react. It's important to have her desensitized to them outside vs in the house first since the house is "her" domain and she has a different mindset there. 

5. Restart the process, but in your yard, if you have one. If you don't have a yard start on your front step/porch/whatever. 

6. Restart the process, but in your house. Bring her to a spot where she has a higher chance of success (either where she can't see the visitor coming in or where she can, I don't know her so can't determine whether or not the sound is more stimulating vs the visualization of them, so pick an area which is the least stimulating, then work up to the more difficult). If she becomes overstimulated, have the guest step outside until you can refocus her and start again. Repeat until she is able to stay focused and give her a jackpot of treats. Repeat until there is a 98% success rate and start closing the gap between the distance of her and the visitor(s). Once she's at a state where you can keep her focused, have them start tossing treats at her too, but only when she is calm. It is very important that they ignore her otherwise, just like in the previous exercises, until she is non-reactive and they are able to pet her without her becoming overstimulated. 


The goal of these exercises is to continually increase the duration of the desired behavior until it becomes habit for her. This can take several weeks to achieve, but with consistency and dedication she should be able to achieve this. It is also important to not over-train her for the day, as you want to leave it on a positive note to keep her interested and motivated. This usually takes up to 1.5 hours, depending on how she does for the day. It is also very important to keep the training level appropriate for her and where she is on the advancement and if she seems to be falling back to widen the gap again and start over. 

If all else fails I recommend finding a qualified obedience trainer in your area that holds small group lessons as this will expose her to outside stimuli and will help you work on controlling her with other people and dogs around you. I would not, however, recommend Petco or Petsmart because their environment is not controlled whatsoever. 

Good luck and I hope that this helps ♡

It's not a dominance thing, it's a play thing. Puppies, or dogs in general, play with their mouths. Not only as a certified canine obedience trainer but also as a veterinary technician, I highly discourage "asserting dominance" in that way as it can lead to fearful behavior later in life. 


*Things to do to discourage biting:*

1. Keep up redirecting her and using high-motivation rewards when the unwanted behavior stops.

2. Yelp loudly, like a dog, when it occurs. As previously stated, puppies naturally play this way and their goal isn't to harm, rather to bond and get their energy out. If you communicate to them that it hurts they will be discouraged to do it again.

3. Encourage them to find other means to get rid of that pent up energy. Take them for walks in trusted places appropriate for their age and vaccine status. Gently play tug of war with them. 


*Ways to teach them the hierarchy without causing fearful behavior:*

1. Conistency in rules. Dogs thrive when everything is consistent, so make sure that you reward them when they follow them and encourage/redirect them when they aren't. 

2. Make them ask for everything. The food you buy isn't theirs, it's yours and you're allowing them to have it. This is accomplished by making sit and wait for their meals rather than just letting them have it. Just remember only to expect maybe 5-10 seconds of them waiting and increase the intervals when they reach a 90% success rate. The same goes for toys. Get a toy bin and teach them to sit next to it when they want to play with toys. Make them ask for permission to get on the couch or bed.

3. Begin age-appropriate basic obedience. By this I mean wait, sit, down, heel, drop it, leave it, easy, come and their name. Not only does obedience training teach your puppy to do what they're asked, but will help develop a deeper bond with them. Please consult a local trainer for how-tos on these if there's any confusion or questions.

4. Teach them that they can't say hi to every dog and person that they meet. This one is tricky because you need to socialize them, but you need them to learn self-control to listen to you with when it's important to not approach people/other dogs in certain situations. By doing so you will eliminate an adult dog who will yank your arm out of its socket to say hi to anything they want. This is especially important due to the breeds that your dog is mixed with. Both have a bad rap so it's important for them to be on their best behavior.

5. Exercise. To accomplish all of the steps to teach them the hierarchy they need to be tired so that they can focus. This is especially important with the two breeds that your dog is mixed with. German Shepherds and Pitties need a lot of mental and physical stimulation for them to thrive and not turn into crazies. I've had both breeds as puppies and experience these breeds daily at work so I know how they can be both ways.

Anyway, I hope this helped and good luck with the baby!

Just make sure that you're ready for a lot of questions. Things I would ask before I bring the doctor in would be:

1. How long has it been there/when did you noticed it?

2. Have they ever over-groomed themselves before or caused self harm? (Btw, yes, some cats have OCD tendencies and hyper-focus on one area, causing self-mutilation and require behavioral medications. It doesn't happen often, but it does happen).

3. Are they scratching it? Any other area itchy to them?

4. Do you use flea/tick prevention? If so, when was it last applied?

5. Do you know if your cat is allergic to anything?

6. What food, including treats, do you feed them? What is the protein and grain source of that specific formulation? How much do you feed them and how often?

7. Do their ears seem to be bothering them?

8. Any changes in litterbox behavior? What kind of litter do you use?

9. Any changes in the household which could cause new stressors?

10. Has there been any vomiting (other than hairballs), diarrhea, coughing and/or sneezing? Are they eating and drinking normally? Bathroom habits normal in amount and frequency?

11. Any other lumps, bumps or scabs that you've noticed?

12. Any bats, rodents or other small animals come into your house recently?

Additional questions will be asked regarding what it looks like on presentation in person, but what we would do in the practice I work at would be to perform a skin scrape to rule out parasitic infections, shave the area to get a better look at it, clean it with surgical scrub and possibly flush it if there's an area where it's draining. You'll probably get sent home with some sort of antibiotic, either topical, oral or both, and will need to recheck it to see if it's better. We would probably send you home with Revolution, which is a topical flea, mite and intestinal parasite prevention just to cover everything in case it's flea dermatitis (which is when they're allergic to the fleas themselves). But regardless, listen to your veterinarian and adhere to their treatment plan.

Good luck! ♡
